Built on a tight urban plot, vibration-free (CFA).

Not watertight.
If the soil is not stable on its own, but no watertightness is needed.

Vibration-free, stiff wall.

Compared with a diaphragm wall, economical only in special cases.

Cantilever wall (no separate support)
As a cantilever it is stable only to an excavation depth of about 4–6 m.
In a narrow trench, bracing (shoring) is simpler.
At small depth the embedment (passive earth resistance) is enough.
Borderline: 4–6 m.
With a structure right beside it, the movement of a cantilever wall is too large.
Internal strutting (cross-bracing, raking struts)
In a narrow trench the two soil faces can be braced against each other.
Above about 3 m the struts buckle: bracing in several directions or raking struts are needed.
Awkward in a wide excavation – tubular struts or anchors are needed.

Not needed for a narrow trench.

Permanent anchor: stricter corrosion protection, re-stressing possible.
It can run into a basement or a utility – they have to be mapped first.
For such a span a tubular strut is no longer economical (splicing, intermediate support).
In a narrow trench simple shoring is enough.
Unnecessary at small depth.
Typical support for tight, nearly right-angled excavations, underpasses, metro stations.
For long tubes, thermal expansion and buckling govern.
Economical if anchoring is not possible.
A stiff system: small wall movement beside a sensitive neighbour.
Hinders excavation and the construction of the internal structure.
Supporting slab (top-down / Milan method)
The slabs are permanent parts of the building – not for a temporary excavation.
At small depth the complicated technology is not worth it.
In deep basements the slabs provide very stiff support as diaphragms.
Small wall movement beside sensitive neighbours.

Trench boxes, sunk while digging
Vertical planking: first we dig to full depth

In fine sand shoring is compulsory above 0,5 m already, and m₀ is much smaller than the 2,5 m depth – so vertical planking (digging to full depth without support) is ruled out. Trench boxes can be lifted in quickly, reused many times, and when sunk, the face is never left unsupported. There is no room for a slope, and nailing is not for trenches.
